Article Title: ‘I got it late, but I got it’: Told she was too old, Suchika Tariyal went from judo, kurash and ju-jitsu to Asian Games MMA bronze
Article Text:
Suchika Tariyal

Suchika Tariyal

The girl who wanted to learn how to fight

Another sport, another beginning

Suchika MMA

Suchika with her husband Kapil

The 700 grams

Suchika first Indian athlete to win an Asian Games medal in Mixed Martial Arts (MMA)

The gym where Suchika Tariyal trains is modest: a single floor, a makeshift mat, a cage and the equipment needed to prepare for mixed martial arts. It is owned by Vikas Dahiya, an MMA fighter himself. When Dahiya is out of town, the keys are with Tariyal and her husband, Kapil Hooda.The couple have become so invested in the place that it is more than a training facility. It is part of the routine around which they have organised their lives, with Kapil closely watching his wife's preparation and sharing the emotional highs and lows of her career.For years, that routine was built around a goal that kept slipping out of reach. Tariyal moved from one combat sport to another, dealt with selection hurdles, and came close to walking away more than once. The medal she had chased since childhood finally arrived at 36, when she became India's first Asian Games medallist in MMA.“For me, it's more than my life. Because I had a dream since childhood, which has come true today. I mean, I got it late, but I got it. I am very happy about it. I can't believe I have achieved it.I still can't believe it. But I feel like I have to do more. That's what's in my mind.”The bronze was a first for Indian MMA. Tariyal, though, was still thinking about the final she had missed. The semifinal against Singapore’s Hui Hoon Teo went to an additional round and was decided by a weigh-in tiebreak. Tariyal was 700 grams heavier and missed the final.“But I missed a gold medal. I was very sad. I had planned to win gold. But it did not happen. I am very sad about it.”The disappointment was familiar. Her sporting career had been marked by moments when she came close to a breakthrough, only for circumstances to push her towards another route. Judo had been her first sport, followed by kurash and ju-jitsu, before MMA gave her another chance at an Asian Games medal.The medal also carried the memory of a time when she had considered walking away altogether.“I had a desire from my childhood, which I made my life and I didn't achieve - either Commonwealth or Asian Games or Olympics. I wanted to get a medal. I wanted people to know about my struggling life, or how I reached here, or how my family helped me reach here.”Tariyal grew up in Chhawla, near Najafgarh in Delhi, one of four sisters. Her introduction to combat sports came not from a dream of winning medals or building an international career, but from an experience that left her feeling vulnerable as a child.When she was around 12 and sporting a ‘boy cut’, a barber at a salon touched her inappropriately. She returned home without telling her family what had happened, frightened and unsure how to process the incident. The experience stayed with her and eventually shaped her decision to learn how to fight back.“The barber touched me wrongly. I felt very bad. I did not know what was going on. I did not know why this happened to me.”“I did not tell anyone. I did not tell my family. I did not want to go out. I did not want to play. I did not know what to do. I wanted to learn a fighting game, so that if this happens again, I can do it.”Her mother eventually enrolled her in judo. Tariyal had wanted to learn boxing, but she took to judo quickly.“I was crazy about it. I didn't want to study or do anything. I just wanted to play judo. I wanted to give my 100% in judo.”She became an eight-time national judo champion. She won silver at the 2018 Commonwealth Judo Championships, gold at the 2019 edition and gold at the 2019 South Asian Games.Tariyal spent 15 years in judo and tried to qualify for the Olympics, but the Covid-19 pandemic disrupted that pursuit. At the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, she lost the bronze-medal bout in the final seconds.The route to the Asian Games through judo had also become difficult. Ranking requirements made selection challenging, so she turned to kurash, which offered another pathway.She trained for around a year and won the selection trials, but her name was not cleared for the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou until the final days before the competition.“Due to two federations, we were left behind. I didn’t have my name on the list. At that time, Mr Anurag Thakur was the sports minister. He helped us a lot. He made us understand. He listened to us. I got my name in the last moment, but I didn’t get enough training because we were running to get my name cleared.”She competed in kurash at Hangzhou but lost.After leaving kurash, Tariyal took up ju-jitsu and became a world champion in 2024. But the achievement did not guarantee a clear path forward, with the sport’s recognition in India remaining an obstacle. MMA offered another route, giving her a fresh opportunity to pursue the Asian Games medal she had long wanted.Pooja Tomar and Himanshu Kaushik encouraged her to try the sport. Tomar is a trailblazer in Indian MMA: she became the first Indian woman to compete in the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) in June 2024, and the first Indian fighter to win a bout in the promotion. Kaushik also guided Tariyal towards the sport.Tomar's presence is not limited to that early advice. She lives one floor above Tariyal and Kapil in their apartment complex on the outskirts of Gurugram. The proximity is part of the small circle around the fighter, a network of people who have encouraged her to continue when other routes have closed.Because of her judo background, she was comfortable with grappling but had to develop her striking. “I am a grappler. I have a judo background. It was difficult for me. I wanted to learn striking,” she said.She gradually worked on the new skills and that transition also opened a route into professional MMA. Tariyal signed a five-fight deal with BRAVE Combat Federation, making her promotional debut at BRAVE CF 92 in Bahrain in December 2024.The deal offered a way to continue competing professionally while she pursued the Asian Games pathway. Tariyal said she had completed two fights under the contract, with three remaining. Her judo background also shaped her choice of traditional MMA for the Asian Games, where the use of a gi (Judogi) and the emphasis on grappling and throws suited her strengths.Tariyal's career has involved repeated reinvention and each change required her to adapt her training and start again, often without the certainty that the new discipline would bring the medal she wanted. But the setbacks were not only about results or injuries. As she grew older, she began hearing a different kind of criticism: that she was too old to continue.Kapil, who works in Manesar, had seen how much Tariyal had given to sport. By the time they married, she had a job and a home, but years of chasing a major medal had left her close to giving up. Kapil urged her to continue, even as the financial burden of keeping her career going grew.“My husband had faith in me. I had given up. I was married and had a good job. I had a house and a husband. Then he believed in me, that I can do it. ‘I have seen you doing it,’” Tariyal said.Keeping her career going cost money. She took unpaid leave from work to train and compete, while overseas camps and travel had to be paid for without any guarantee of a result.“He spent from his pocket, took loans and he trained me. He sent me to Bali. I went there three-four times for two months. I have a job, and when I go for training, I go without pay. I don't get paid. Whatever I needed, he spent it.”Kapil approached people for financial help, but was repeatedly told that Tariyal was too old to continue. Eventually, he stopped asking and concentrated on doing what he could himself.Tariyal also looked for ways to find sponsors. During COVID-19, she appeared on reality television, hoping the exposure might help fund training and competition.“I thought if I do two-four events, I might get a sponsor,” she said. “If I get a sponsor, I will do it.”However, she dislocated her elbow during one of the shows. The injury put her preparation for the 2022 Commonwealth Games at risk. Even though she recovered in time to compete, she decided not to return to reality shows until she had achieved her sporting goals.“I decided I won't go to such reality shows until I achieve. I have to focus on my work,” she said.The doubts about her age continued. Tariyal said she heard at training camps that she should step aside and give younger athletes a chance.“A lot of people meet me and say that you have become so old. You have become 30 years old. You can’t play [the sport],” she said. “We still get to hear in the camps that you are too old. You shouldn't play now. You should drop now. You should give a chance to the youth ahead. So, I have heard this many times.”Her response was to keep competing. “As long as my body is working or I want to play, I can play. And you have seen that I have won a medal,” she said. “The more demotivating people I met in my life, the more motivated I got.”When she moved into MMA, Tariyal said, the federation - MMA-SFI (Mixed Martial Arts Sports Federation of India) - helped with training, food and other requirements and allowed her to use its gym without monthly fees.“I haven't seen such a federation,” she said.She credits Kapil with helping her stay in sport long enough to reach the Asian Games podium. “I would like to thank him. That's why I reached here. It was his dream, which I fulfilled.”At Aichi-Nagoya, the pressure of the opening bout was clear to Tariyal. She admitted to her coach that she was scared, only for him to tell her that he felt the same way, but believed she would do well.“I was very nervous at that time. I told my coach that I was scared. He said, ‘It's fair. You are scared, so you are telling the truth.’ I said, ‘Yes, I am scared.’ He said, ‘It's okay, I am scared too. But you will do well. I know you have worked very hard.’”She focused on winning the quarterfinal and securing a medal. “I had a belief that I have to win this round. Only then I will be able to secure a medal. I played all out. I don't know how I performed in the first round. I was very disturbed. Will my body work or not? What kind of performance will come? I played and I won. I was very happy.”The win assured her of bronze. The semifinal tiebreak kept her out of the final by 700 grams. At 36, Tariyal had finally won the Asian Games medal she had wanted since childhood.For now, Tariyal’s focus shifts to the World Championships in November. She will travel to Mumbai to prepare for the event, while the two remaining bouts on her BRAVE Combat Federation contract remain on the back burner.
Article Summary: Suchika Tariyal is the first Indian athlete to win an Asian Games medal in Mixed Martial Arts (MMA) The 36-year-old missed the final because she was 700 grams heavier. Her introduction to combat sports came not from a dream of winning medals, but from an experience that left her feeling vulnerable.

Article Title: Opaque selection, forced doubles pairing: Para-shuttlers challenge Para Asian Games non-selection in Delhi HC
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Chirag Baretha is a two-time Asian Games medallist, having won silver in 2023 and bronze in 2018. Instead of focusing on the upcoming Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, which begin on October 18, he is running from pillar to post, trying to keep his fading dream of representing India alive. The 29-year-old has also won bronze medals at the 2024 BWF Para Badminton World Championships, the 2025 Asian Para Badminton Championships, and the 2026 World Para Badminton Championships.Baretha, alongside fellow para-shuttlers Shashank Kumar, Ammu Mohan and Manisha Patel, has filed a petition in the Delhi High Court against the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports (MYAS), the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI), the Badminton Association of India (BAI) and the Sports Authority of India (SAI) over their non-selection.In the petition, accessed by TimesofIndia.com, the para-shuttlers argue that they meet the selection criteria set by the Sports Ministry, which require them to be ranked in the top six in Asia. Baretha and Mandeep Kaur were ranked World No. 6 in the SL3-SU5 category on July 14, 2026, when the rankings were considered for the Asian Para Games.Subsequently, the petition argues that " Rakesh Pandey has not obtained or won any medal in the last 12 months or have ranking less than the petitioners in the international athlete ranking.Moreover, he was debarred for 4 years for failing the Anti-Doping Test."The men's doubles pairing of Rakesh Pandey and Dev Rathi was ranked World No. 3 in the SU5 category on the cutoff date. However, Rakesh is set to partner Umesh Vikram Kumar in men's doubles at the Asian Para Games, while also finding a spot in the men's singles discipline.This, too, has a layer of intrigue. In an email sent to qualified para-shuttlers on August 25, K Prabhakar Rao , the chairman of para-badminton at the Badminton Association of India (BAI), made it clear that "for a pair to be considered valid for recommendation, separate emails must be received from both players, with each player naming the other as their partner for the concerned event."In response, Baretha, who was named in the Badminton World Federation's (BWF) entry list, registered for singles (SU5 category), men's doubles (SU5 with Hardik Makkar) and mixed doubles (SL3-SU5 with Mandeep Kaur).However, Vikram, Pandey's partner at the Asian Para Games, expressed displeasure at his name being added to the doubles draw without his consent. "Sir, I have not given consent to participate in MD SL3 SU5. How can I [sic] my name appear in doubles? Please make sure to remove my name from doubles without affecting my singles entry," he wrote in a WhatsApp group for Asian Para Games athletes. He addressed the message to Prabhakar Rao and coach Venkata Murali Krishna.However, his plea was not entertained. "Vikram, we can discuss this in a physical meeting at hotel. At this stage, no modification is allowed. We already discussed with referee, ABC [Asian Badminton Confederation] persons."Not satisfied, Vikram responded, "Sir, I will be arriving at hotel late tonight and by that time draw will be announced. Without my consent, my name should not be entered. Pandey bhaiya can play with Hardik (Makkar)."For Vikram, there is no way out. The rules stipulate that if a player withdraws from one discipline, they withdraw from the entire tournament.This sequence of events, and the eventual loss of his place in the contingent, has left Baretha distraught."We are (fighting) on a merit basis. We are medal holders. We are rank holders. We followed the guidelines of SAI. But Mr Prabhakar Rao has tricked us and affected our career and effort of four years," Baretha told TimesofIndia.com."I am Asia No. 6 and have qualified through my ranking. Even if you ignore that, I meet another clause of being a medallist from previous Games. The same applied to Suhas (Lalinakere Yathiraj), who was not in the top six but had won a medal the last time [gold].""Before my name was withdrawn at the manager's meeting, the draw was such that I was destined to reach the final. Except for one player, I have been able to beat everyone. I could guarantee the country a silver medal," he added confidently.K Prabhakar Rao said the squad selection was not theirs to make in the first place."The Badminton Association of India didn't have a say in this. We didn't include or exclude an athlete as per our choices. We got this list from SAI, and we followed it," he told TimesofIndia.com.The exclusion of former head coach Gaurav Khanna is believed to have been a major factor in the entire selection fracas. Khanna, who established India's first para-badminton academy (Gaurav Khanna Excellia Badminton Academy), has the likes of Suhas and Baretha under his wing.Baretha alleged that senior para-shuttlers were instrumental in creating a negative impression of Khanna among officials at SAI. "These senior athletes have set a wrong aura in front of the Sports Authority of India. They have also harmed me. It includes Sukant Kadam, Nitesh Kumar, Pramod Bhagat and Rakesh Pandey himself.""They keep going on about the academy, but at least look at my credentials. Look at my medals, my ranking. I am talking about my achievements."In the days following the squad announcement and Baretha's omission on October 12, Baretha, Shashank Kumar and Ammu Mohan approached the Delhi High Court and met Dr Pallavi Rai, SAI's director (TEAMS Division), but failed to receive a satisfactory response. Their repeated attempts to seek clarity from BAI secretary Sanjay Mishra and K Prabhakar Rao have also failed to yield results.The para-shuttlers are not the only aggrieved group of Indian athletes. Para-shooters and para-cyclists, too, had demanded a fairer and more transparent selection process. They held a protest during the send-off ceremony on October 8.India has sent a 281-member contingent to the Asian Para Games, which includes 168 athletes.The Sports Ministry issues selection criteria for the Asian Games and Asian Para Games.BAI reiterates the selection criteria for the Asian Para Games.SAI announces the contingent for the Asian Para Games.Para-shuttlers converge in Delhi to travel to the Games.Chirag Baretha, Shashank Kumar, Ammu Mohan and Manisha Patel file a petition in the Delhi High Court over their non-selection.Para-shuttlers report in Aichi-Nagoya.Badminton begins at the Asian Para Games.The Asian Para Games are officially opened.
Article Summary: Chirag Baretha is a two-time Asian Games medallist, having won silver in 2023 and bronze in 2018. The 29-year-old has also won bronze medals at the 2024 BWF Para Badminton World Championships. Baretha, alongside fellow para-shuttlers Shashank Kumar, Ammu Mohan and Manisha Patel, has filed a petition in the Delhi High Court.

Article Text:

Sonipat's Winners

Sonipat’s Gold Medal Winners [13]

When Kushal Dalal picked up boxing gloves, his family didn’t say no. When he gave that up and decided on archery – because Kushal didn’t like the idea of hitting anyone and felt at home in “a peaceful sport” – they agreed to that, too. There was no place around to practise archery, so a section of the family’s 5-acre farmland at Siwanka village in Sonipat was cleared. Paddy straw was woven to give him targets.Village gossip had brought Kiran Pahal’s running days to an abrupt end. After talk of Kiran “speaking to a boy” reached her father, he stopped her from going out. He relented after Kiran went on a hunger strike. Her grandmother used money from her pension to buy her a pair of running shoes.Before Neha Goyal played hockey for India, she helped her mother and sisters fix bicycles. Neha was eight when a friend told her hockey players got free shoes, clothes and notebooks. Her mother, who worked in houses and at a foam factory, didn’t stop her from playing.At the recently concluded Asian Games in Japan’s Aichi-Nagoya, a neighbour of Delhi reaped possibly India’s biggest harvest for a single city. Each of these stories – and 10 more like these – culminated in a gold medal.Each began, and blossomed, in Sonipat.Though in NCR, Sonipat doesn’t have Delhi’s influence, Gurgaon’s money or Noida’s infrastructure. As a manufacturing hub of auto components and ancillaries that are used in the domestic market and abroad, Sonipat has so far been writing its script, literally, in parts.Sport, which bubbles in its DNA, works much in the same way – many individual parts that don’t get to show their prowess as a sum. Aichi-Nagoya was that rare instance when they did. Serendipity? Perhaps. Organisation? Possible. Talent? Certainly.But talent needs spotting. And for virtually all the gold medallists, that was someone in the family who made it possible, sometimes with a push, sometimes with a quiet sacrifice –a family clearing land, a grandmother spending her pension, a mother working to buy shoes, a coach paying school fees for a stranger’s daughter.The other aspect of the Japan feat that places Sonipat apart from traditional sporting nurseries like Bhiwani (boxing) is the diversity of the 13 (individual and team combined) gold medals that athletes from here won, across disciplines like hockey, archery, kabaddi , athletics and wrestling.Serendipity did play a part. For several of these medallists, sport wasn’t the original dream. Neha Goyal, midfielder in the gold-winning women’s hockey team, started going for hockey classes after a friend told her hockey players received free shoes, clothes and notebooks. She joined because her family needed those things. Some families saw sport as a way to support the child’s education; others came to see it as a route eventually to a govt job.Coaches TOI spoke to said access to proper training remains the difference between a talent lost and a talent realised. Sonipat’s sportspersons have certainly benefited from its concentration of sports institutions and training centres around Rai and Bahalgarh. It has a Sports Authority of India (SAI) National Centre of Excellence, a residential sports school and Sports University of Haryana . The SAI centre covers 83 acres and its listed facilities include a 70-metre archery field, a floodlit synthetic athletics track, synthetic hockey fields, two mud kabaddi courts, wrestling halls, a sports injury and rehabilitation centre, a hypoxic chamber and hostels.Motilal Nehru School of Sports at Rai, founded by Haryana govt in 1973, has athletics, archery, weightlifting, wrestling and swimming among its competencies.Village akharas, kabaddi nurseries and private academies sit in different parts of the access route. One such academy, run by former India hockey captain Pritam Rani Siwach and her husband, has produced a steady stream of national hockey players. Seven hockey players from Sonipat were part of the men’s and women’s Indian teams that won gold at Aichi-Nagoya: four women and three men. All four women and one in the men’s team (Pritam Rani’s son Yashdeep) trained at the academy, which now has around 200 players, 150 of them girls.Among the youngest there is Ritika. The five-year-old is still mastering her numbers and alphabets in school but is quickly picking up dribbling and promptly agreed to show this reporter the right grip for the hockey stick. “Aise pakadte hain. Aur phir ball ko goal mein daalna hota hai. Jo ball andar daalega, woh jeetega! (this is how you hols the stick. The objective is to score a goal with the ball. Whoever does that wins)” she said.When Pritam Rani started the academy in 2004, she had seven trainees. When the academy paid school fees and helped buy shoes and other equipment, more began to join. I never wanted money to become the reason a talented girl stopped playing,” she told TOI. Food mattered, too. Many girls came from families for whom milk and fruit were luxuries, so the academy began providing soaked chana, milk and bananas.Neha, who came for the shoes, stayed for the dream – of building a house for her mother. “I did not start playing hockey thinking I wanted to play for India. I was in Class IV when a friend told me about the shoes, clothes and notebooks,” she said. “There were people who told my mother to keep me at home. But she never stopped me.” A cash prize for being player of the match changed her attitude towards hockey. “That Rs 2,000 changed something inside me. I started thinking if I played well, I could earn. Then on, hockey was not just a game for me. It became my responsibility,” she said.Abhishek Nain’s first reason for playing hockey was less ambitious. He was nine when he followed a classmate to a ground because it was an excuse to bunk. His father,, asked him to consider quitting hockey – which he was playing at the national level – after a series of injuries and focus on getting a govt job. Coaches persuaded the family to let him continue. Years later, at Aichi-Nagoya, he would score India’s winning goal against Pakistan in the Asiad semi-final.Seeing girls running on a track outside her school drew Kiran into athletics so much that she began sprinting in her school shoes and slippers, sometimes even barefoot. “I did not know where this would take me or that I would one day be wearing the India badge. I just liked running and wanted to try.” She joined Indian Railways in 2021, gaining financial stability after years of training. “For an athlete, knowing that there is a secure job gives a lot of confidence,” said Kiran, who won the 4x400m relay team gold in Japan.Meenu Beniwal, president of Haryana Olympic Association, linked Sonipat’s sporting culture to shrinking landholdings and search for livelihoods beyond farming. “As ancestral landholdings have shrunk and farming has become less viable for many families, sports have emerged as an important pathway to secure govt jobs and build a better future,” she said. Proximity to Delhi and recruitment opportunities in the Army, Railways, paramilitary forces and other central government departments have also encouraged young people to pursue sport, she felt.Sports University of Haryana vice-chancellor Ashok Kumar said ambitious parents have helped build the ecosystem by investing their own money and taking risks for their children. Institutions have added to that support, creating a baseline sporting infrastructure framework in the city. The university admitsstudents each year, and Sonipat accounts for aroundof admissions.Kabaddi player Pardeep Narwal says children in villages such as Rindhana grow up watching neighbours, relatives and seniors succeed in the sport. Local grounds and kabaddi academies run by former players bring large numbers of youngsters into the sport. In Rindhana alone, around 300 children practise across three grounds, he said.“From my village alone 25-30 athletes have played in Pro Kabaddi League,” Narwal said. Seeing other athletes succeed encourages more children in the village to try. “Family members motivate the kids. They look at a neighbour’s son succeeding and ask their own children why they can’t do the same,” he said.Wrestler Naveen Mor describes the same process in akharas, with local dangals giving children competitive experience early. “When an entire community encourages a sport, the chances of producing champions naturally increase,” said Mor, who runs a wrestling academy on a one-acre plot near Murthal, where he trains 70-80 children. He said he does not charge them because talent may emerge from families unable to afford expensive coaching.“Many of our athletes come from humble farming families, where children grow up helping with physical work and learn discipline, endurance and the value of hard work early in life. Wrestling also offered generations of youngsters from middle-class families a way to build a career, earn recognition and secure a govt job.Earlier, choices for many such families were limited, and sports became a route to a better future. Over time, this created a strong sporting culture, with akharas, coaches, families and former wrestlers all contributing to the next generation,” Mor said.The same may now be happening for hockey and athletics. Maybe, it takes a village to keep producing gold medallists.Women’s HockeyNeha GoyalJyotiSakshi RanaShilpi DabasMen’s HockeySumitAbhishek NainYashdeep SiwachAthleticsKiran PahalArcheryKushal DalalKabaddiSunil KumarAshu MalikRajraniWrestlingSujeet Kalkal
Article Summary: Sonipat, in Haryana, won 13 gold medals at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. The city is a manufacturing hub of auto components and ancillaries that are used in the domestic market and abroad. For virtually all the gold medallists, that was someone in the family who made it possible.

Article Title: ‘Having batting till No.8 is not bravery’: Former India batter slams Shreyas Iyer’s team selection
Article Text:

Former India batter Mohammad Kaif has questioned India’s team combination after Shreyas Iyer and his side suffered a 24-run defeat to West Indies in the fourth T20I in Hyderabad, arguing that the management prioritised batting depth over a stronger bowling attack.India entered the contest with four specialist bowlers and two all-rounders, but the combination failed to contain the West Indies batters, who piled up 247/3 in their 20 overs. The hosts responded with an aggressive batting effort but could manage only 223 before being bowled out, allowing the visitors to level the five-match series 2-2.Kaif felt India’s selection was not suited to the conditions and said the team needed to rely on specialist bowlers rather than expect its batting line-up to compensate for a lack of bowling options."Having batting till No.8 is not bravery. Bravery is playing your proper bowlers on a good batting wicket. A brave call is one where you pick seven batters and five proper bowlers, including Axar Patel as the all-rounder. Bravery is not allowing the opposition to score 250 and then saying we'll chase it down. If you actually play with five main bowlers, you won't need to chase so many. The flatter the conditions, the more specialist bowlers should play," Kaif said on Cricbuzz.India’s difficulties with the ball have been evident across the series. They were unable to defend a target of 250 in the second T20I, while they conceded 209 in the third match despite securing a 14-run win. The latest defeat further highlighted their struggles to restrict the West Indies batting line-up.Kaif also questioned India’s decision to leave out Kuldeep Yadav , arguing that the left-arm wrist-spinner could have offered a valuable wicket-taking option on the Hyderabad surface. He suggested that India should have considered sacrificing an extra batter to improve the balance of the side."I would have played Kuldeep Yadav. Rashid Khan made a name for himself on this Hyderabad track only. The top 4 in the ICC rankings are all leg-spinners. So on a flat track, Kuldeep Yadav would have been even more useful," he said.Kaif added that the pitch conditions could have worked in Kuldeep’s favour, with changes of pace and additional bounce potentially helping the spinner trouble the opposition batters."Just the change of pace and the extra bounce from the Hyderabad pitch would have assisted him. India could have easily dropped a batter and picked another bowler," he added.The series is now level at 2-2, leaving both teams with one match to decide the outcome. The fifth and final T20I will be played at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium in Bengaluru on Saturday.
Article Summary: Mohammad Kaif questions India’s team combination after fourth T20I defeat. Former India batter argues that the management prioritised batting depth over a stronger bowling attack. India entered the contest with four specialist bowlers and two all-rounders, but the combination failed to contain the West Indies batters.

Article Title: ‘Too ambitious’: Ex-India cricketer flags concerns over Gautam Gambhir’s India game plan
Article Text:

Former India batter Wasim Jaffer believes Rinku Singh’s absence is hurting India in the ongoing T20I series against the West Indies, arguing that the left-hander could have made a difference in the fourth match.India suffered a 24-run defeat on Wednesday after the visitors successfully defended a target of 248 to level the five-match series at 2-2. Shai Hope led the charge with an unbeaten 102 off 50 balls as the West Indies finished at 247/3. India, in reply, were bowled out for 223 in 19.3 overs, with Arshdeep Singh retiring hurt in the final over as the chase came to an end.Speaking on his YouTube channel, Jaffer questioned the decision to leave Rinku out of the Indian side, insisting that the batter's ability to deliver in the middle and lower order makes him a valuable option."If you look from a batter's perspective, Rinku is miles ahead of everyone else. He bats amazingly at number five and six, plus he is a left-hander. I feel it is very unfortunate that he is not part of this Indian team purely because he cannot bowl. I can understand Rajat's (Patidar) case, as he bats in the top order and there is no place there, but Rinku should be there," Jaffer said.The former India batter felt Rinku could have given India a chance to turn the game around during the fourth T20I, pointing to the finisher's record in franchise cricket."If you had Rinku in that position, you never know. He could have changed the game. He has the capacity and has won a lot of matches in franchise cricket in this manner," he added.Rinku has struggled to secure a regular place in India's playing XI and was eventually left out of the squad after the Zimbabwe tour. His numbers this year have been modest, with 152 runs from 13 matches at an average of 25.33 and a strike rate of 139.44. His highest score in that period is 44 not out.However, his record when batting at No. 5 or 6 in T20Is tells a different story. In 22 innings in those positions, Rinku has scored 518 runs at an average of 43.15 and a strike rate of 156.00, underlining his effectiveness in the role Jaffer believes he should be given.Jaffer also assessed India's decision to include Naman Dhir in the T20I side, expressing reservations about expecting the all-rounder to bowl his full quota of four overs. He said off-spinners can struggle outside the powerplay when they lack variations, particularly on Indian pitches."It is a bit difficult for off-spinners to bowl after the powerplay if you don't have variety. Roston Chase does it; credit to him. If you do not have that cleverness or variation, especially in India, it becomes very difficult. So to expect that Naman Dhir will bowl four overs is too ambitious," he said.Jaffer added that Dhir's contribution with the bat would be crucial to his place in the T20I side. The all-rounder has managed just 14 runs across three innings in the series, but Jaffer believes he has the ability to provide a quick contribution."I feel his performance with the bat is very important for him to play T20 cricket. Unfortunately, that has not happened in the last two matches, but he has the capability to come and play a quick 25-30 cameo," he signed off.With the series tied at 2-2, India and the West Indies will face off in the fifth and final T20I in Bengaluru on Saturday, October 17.
Article Summary: India suffered a 24-run defeat on Wednesday after the visitors successfully defended a target of 248. Shai Hope led the charge with an unbeaten 102 off 50 balls as the West Indies finished at 247/3. India, in reply, were bowled out for 223 in 19.3 overs, with Arshdeep Singh retiring hurt in the final over.

Article Title: ‘Series in India brings nothing to West Indies’: Cricket’s bilateral revenue model sparks debate
Article Text:
West Indies tour of India (AP Photo)

How the revenue system changed

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Cricket West Indies (CWI) CEO Chris Dehring has questioned the financial system governing bilateral cricket, explaining how it has contributed to the board’s ongoing financial difficulties. Despite the West Indies currently playing a T20I series against India, Dehring said the Caribbean board would not receive any revenue from the series, even as the hosts stand to earn millions.The T20I series is level at 2-2 following Shai Hope’s century in Hyderabad. Speaking to The Scoop by Wisden Cricket, Dehring explained that the financial model leaves visiting teams without a share of the broadcasting revenue generated by bilateral matches."West Indies cricket receives nothing in this case, because the series is being played in India," said Dehring. "A series that could generate $20 million to $30 million in India brings West Indies cricket no revenue."Dehring traced the problem back to 1997, when nine of the 10 ICC member countries voted to change cricket’s financial model. Before that decision, host nations generally paid visiting teams a guaranteed fee, which sometimes earned the West Indies more than hosting matches at home."To understand how this happened, you have to go back to 1997," he added. "I was fortunate, or unfortunate, to be around when the ICC member countries voted to change the financial model that underpinned world cricket. Until then, West Indies was a very attractive team, and everybody wanted us to tour. We would receive a touring fee, which was often worth more than we could earn by hosting a series in the Caribbean."Under the revised system, the country hosting a bilateral series could retain all the revenue generated from its broadcasting rights. Dehring argued that this created a major imbalance between countries with large audiences and smaller cricketing nations."That meant India could retain the revenues generated by a population of one and a half billion people, while West Indies could retain whatever revenues we could generate in Antigua, with its population of around 100,000, or St Kitts, with around 30,000," Dehring continued."It was palpably unfair. We were outvoted nine to one by the ICC member countries. At the time, I said that this decision had effectively signed the demise of West Indies cricket because it took away our main source of income," he added.
Article Summary: Cricket West Indies (CWI) CEO Chris Dehring has questioned the financial system governing bilateral cricket. The financial model leaves visiting teams without a share of the broadcasting revenue generated by bilateral matches. The West Indies are currently playing a T20I series against India, which the hosts stand to earn millions.

Article Title: China’s stapled visa row costs Arunachal weightlifter shot at World Championships
Article Text:
India China

New Delhi: Another sporting flashpoint in India-China ties has cost weightlifter Charu Pesi a shot at the world stage, with the Indian Weightlifting Federation (IWLF) withdrawing the Arunachal Pradesh athlete from the upcoming Senior World Weightlifting Championships in Ningbo after Chinese authorities indicated that he would be issued a stapled visa.Sources told TOI that the Chinese Visa Application Service Centre (CVASS) here sought an undertaking from the Indian federation confirming Pesi’s acceptance of the visa.The IWLF consulted government officials, who maintained that India does not recognise stapled visas issued by China to residents of Arunachal Pradesh. The federation subsequently decided against sending the men’s 65kg lifter to the championships, which begin on Oct 24.An eight-member Indian squad, led by Olympic medallist Mirabai Chanu , is scheduled to compete in Ningbo, with visa processing for the rest of the contingent continuing as usual.Unlike a regular visa stamped on a passport, a stapled visa is issued on a separate piece of paper. Beijing’s practice of issuing such visas to Arunachal Pradesh residents reflects its refusal to recognise India’s sovereignty over the region. India has consistently rejected the practice, viewing it as a challenge to its territorial integrity.This is far from an isolated incident. In July 2023, three Arunachal Pradesh wushu athletes, Nyeman Wangsu, Onilu Tega and Mepung Lamgu, were issued stapled visas for the Summer World University Games in Chengdu. India protested and withdrew its entire wushu contingent.The dispute resurfaced ahead of the Hangzhou Asian Games later that year, when the athletes faced entry and accreditation hurdles, preventing them from competing.For the lifter, it is a bitter setback. The championships would have offered valuable international exposure, with crucial ranking points at stake in the qualification race for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Article Summary: Charu Pesi will not compete at the Senior World Weightlifting Championships in Ningbo. Chinese authorities indicated that he would be issued a stapled visa. Beijing’s practice of issuing such visas to Arunachal Pradesh residents reflects its refusal to recognise India's sovereignty.

Article Title: Three Jharkhand players in India squad for historic lawn bowls series against New Zealand
Article Text:
(From left) Sunil Bahadur, Dinesh Kumar and Reshma Kumari

Kolkata: Three players from Jharkhand will be part of India’s four-member lawn bowls squad for a historic three-Test series against New Zealand in Nov, part of the centenary celebrations of sporting ties between the two countries.Lawn bowls is one of the only four sports, alongside cricket, hockey and football, selected for the centenary programme.2022 Commonwealth Games silver medallists Dinesh Kumar and Sunil Bahadur and rising player Reshma Kumari, all from Jharkhand, have been selected alongside Arjuna Awardee and Commonwealth Games gold medallist Pinki Singh for the series, scheduled from Nov 16-18 in Auckland.“This is a very important event for us because only four sports are taking part in the centenary celebrations. On the days we are playing, no other sport will be taking place, which means we will receive exclusive coverage,” Bowling Federation of India president Ravi Bengani told TOI in an exclusive interview on Thursday.India will play three Test matches over three days, with each Test comprising five matches — men’s pairs, women’s pairs, mixed fours, mixed pairs 1 and mixed pairs 2.The New Zealand series is part of a broader international exposure programme the federation has put in place as it begins preparations for the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad.A 12-member Indian contingent will travel to Malaysia later this month for a World Bowls-sanctioned tournament, while another group will compete in an invitational event in Hong Kong, where Indian players won bronze medals last year.The federation’s confidence has also received a boost from Putul Sonowal’s recent podium finish at the Champion of Champions event, a first for an Indian player at the prestigious competition.“We have decided to participate in as many World Bowls-sanctioned events as possible. International exposure is crucial if we want to bridge the gap with the leading nations,” Bengani said.The federation is also planning to strengthen its support structure through its partnership with Bowls New Zealand. Bengani revealed that India currently does not have a dedicated national coach, making the proposed knowledge-sharing programme particularly significant.“We have signed an agreement with Bowls New Zealand and now we will have more exchange programmes. We will bring their coaches and technical officials to India and provide our players with greater exposure and expertise,” Bengani said.The plans have gained momentum following the federation’s recognition by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports earlier this year, a move expected to improve funding and access to high-performance support.As far as the 2030 Commonwealth Games are concerned, the federation has set ambitious targets. “I’m committing to at least four gold medals for India in 2030. Personally, I feel we can win even more if we continue on the current path,” Bengani said.With a packed international calendar, plans to bring in New Zealand coaches and technical experts, and Ahmedabad 2030 on the horizon, the federation believes Indian lawn bowls is entering its most ambitious phase yet.
Article Summary: Lawn bowls is one of the only four sports, alongside cricket, hockey and football, selected for the centenary programme. India will play three Test matches over three days, with each Test comprising five matches. The series is part of a broader international exposure programme the federation has put in place as it begins preparations for the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad.

Article Title: EFI mess costs Indian riders global stage, FEI ban from Dec 1
Article Text:
Equestrian Federation of India

New Delhi:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Yet another tale of administrative chaos and athletes paying the price. Caught in a prolonged governance crisis at the Equestrian Federation of India (EFI), Indian riders now face a ban from international competitions, with their sporting futures hanging in the balance. The latest setback comes at a time when the govt is pushing to bring more international events to India and widen Indian athletes’ exposure to global competition.The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) has decided to suspend the EFI from Dec 1 over prolonged governance irregularities and failure to hold fresh elections, effectively shutting Indian riders, officials, trainers and horses out of international events. TOI is in possession of FEI’s Oct 15 letter confirming the decision, which was taken at the international body's board meeting on Oct 13.Explaining its move, the FEI said the EFI’s prolonged governance crisis had reached a tipping point. “The absence of elections to date to elect a new Executive Committee, has resulted in a prolonged governance and leadership irregularity that is no longer sustainable,” the letter by FEI Governance Director Francisco Lima stated.The crisis follows the Delhi high court’s dissolution of the EFI executive committee in Feb 2026. Its elected tenure had expired in Sept 2023, while fresh elections remain pending nine months after the court’s intervention. The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) constituted an ad hoc committee on March 27 to oversee the federation and facilitate the electoral process.While acknowledging the committee’s Sept 27 submission and its work, the FEI said elections were expected by Jan 31, 2027. However, the suspension will be reviewed only after the polls are held and evaluated by the international body.The consequences are sweeping. Citing its statutes, the FEI said the EFI “may not attend or be represented at any session or meeting of any FEI body, nor may it organise international events.” More damagingly, athletes, officials, trainers and horses “may not participate in international events organised by the FEI or any other national federation, whether under the Indian flag or the FEI flag.”With the suspension taking effect before the stated election deadline, Indian riders risk losing crucial international competition opportunities. Their return will depend on the completion of elections and the FEI’s subsequent evaluation, leaving athletes caught in a governance crisis they did not create.
Article Summary: The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) has decided to suspend the EFI from Dec 1 over prolonged governance irregularities and failure to hold fresh elections. ToI is in possession of FEI’s Oct 15 letter confirming the decision, which was taken at the international body's board meeting on Oct 13. “The absence of elections to date to elect a new Executive Committee, has resulted in a prolonged governance and leadership irregularity that is no longer sustainable,” the FEI Governance Director Francisco Lima stated.

Article Title: SA vs AUS: Steve Smith cleared of concussion after helmet blow, returns to field in Durban Test

Former Australia captain Steve Smith has been cleared of concussion and resumed fielding duties on the fifth day of the first Test against South Africa at Kingsmead in Durban on Tuesday, after undergoing a series of clinical assessments following a blow to the helmet.The 37-year-old batter was struck by a short-pitched delivery from Anrich Nortje during Australia's second innings. Smith attempted to duck under the ball but misjudged its trajectory as it failed to rise as much as he expected.Although he continued batting after the incident, scoring 27 off 41 balls before being caught at long-on off Simon Harmer, Smith did not take the field when South Africa began their second innings on Monday. Michael Neser served as his substitute fielder during that session.However, Smith returned to the field on Tuesday morning after being cleared under Cricket Australia's concussion protocols. He was stationed in the slip cordon when South Africa resumed their chase and subsequently took a catch to dismiss Kyle Verreynne off Matt Renshaw's bowling."Steve Smith has undergone a series of clinical assessments over the past 24 hours in accordance with Cricket Australia’s concussion protocols and has been cleared to take the field this morning," Cricket Australia said in a statement.The incident brought back memories of Smith's previous concussion scare during the 2019 Ashes in England, when he was struck on the head by fast bowler Jofra Archer and forced to miss part of a Test match.Smith's return to the field came after medical assessments over the preceding 24 hours, with Australia following the prescribed protocols before allowing the experienced batter to resume his duties.His presence was a boost for Australia as they pushed for victory in the series opener, with South Africa mounting a determined resistance on the final day.South Africa resumed at 102/4 on Tuesday, needing another 319 runs to win. They reached 166/6 by lunch after Australia struck twice to strengthen their grip on the contest.Opener Aiden Markram led the home side's resistance, remaining unbeaten on 69 at the interval alongside Marco Jansen on seven. The pair had to rebuild after Wiaan Mulder's patient 69-run fifth-wicket partnership with Markram ended when Josh Hazlewood had Mulder caught behind by Alex Carey.Part-time spinner Matt Renshaw then dismissed Verreynne, who made just one before edging a reckless shot to Smith at slip.Renshaw has been Australia's standout performer with the bat, having scored 190 in the first innings and 82 in the second, before adding two wickets to his match contribution.Australia needed four more wickets at lunch to seal victory in the opening Test. The second Test of the series is scheduled to begin in Gqeberha on Sunday.
Article Summary: Steve Smith cleared of concussion after blow to the helmet. Former Australia captain was struck by short-pitched delivery from Anrich Nortje. Smith took a catch to dismiss Kyle Verreynne off Matt Renshaw's bowling. Australia needed four more wickets at lunch to seal victory in the opening Test.

Article Title: SA20: Faf du Plessis, Rassie van der Dussen headline auction shortlist

The SA20 Season 5 auction will see 156 cricketers go under the hammer on October 7, with former Joburg Super Kings captain Faf du Plessis Rassie van der Dussen and all-rounder Wiaan Mulder among the leading South African names available.The shortlist was trimmed down from 789 players who initially registered for the auction. Of the 156 players remaining, 95 are South African and 61 are overseas cricketers, with 19 squad places still available across four of the six franchises.Durban's Super Giants and Paarl Royals have already completed their 19-player squads and will not participate in the auction. Joburg Super Kings and MI Cape Town have six slots each to fill, while Pretoria Capitals have five and Sunrisers Eastern Cape have two.JSK and MI Cape Town also have the largest purses available, with $1.24 million and $562,813, respectively. Sunrisers Eastern Cape have $216,699 remaining, while Pretoria Capitals have $88,786.Among the leading South African players in the pool are du Plessis, Mulder, fast bowler Nandre Burger and veteran batter van der Dussen. Du Plessis, who previously led JSK, continues to feature prominently in franchise cricket and recently finished as the leading run-scorer in Europe.The two Under-23 slots are also expected to attract significant interest. Fast bowler Matthew Boast, who commanded the joint-highest bid at the Season 2 auction, is among the players in this category, alongside former South Africa Under-19 captain Jason Rowles.The first four SA20 auctions have produced several significant deals. Tristan Stubbs fetched $554,693 at the inaugural auction, while Dewald Brevis set a new record with a $994,834 deal last season.The auction has also provided a route for several South African players to gain exposure to international franchise cricket, with some subsequently securing further opportunities on the global T20 circuit.The overseas contingent includes former West Indies captain Kieron Pollard, New Zealand pacer Trent Boult, Shimron Hetmyer, Shamar Joseph, Mohammad Nabi, AM Ghazanfar, Jordan Cox, Aneurin Donald, Rehan Ahmed and Richard Gleeson.Several established T20 names are already part of the six franchises, including Jos Buttler, Joe Root, Sam Curran, Sunil Narine, Kane Williamson, Andre Russell, Sherfane Rutherford, Mitchell Marsh and Phil Salt.The auction will be broadcast live on SuperSport at 5pm SAST, JioStar at 8.30pm IST, Sky Sports at 4pm BST, Apex at 7.30pm PKT, Fox Sports at 11pm AEDT and Willow TV at 11am ET. The event will also be streamed live on the SA20 YouTube channel.

Former Joburg Super Kings captain Faf du Plessis and all-rounder Wiaan Mulder are among the leading South African names available. Article Title: India’s No. 8 obsession: Why Kuldeep Yadav is caught in the crossfire
Article Text:
India's Kuldeep Yadav (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Over the last 15 months, the No. 8 spot in the batting line-up has been a sensitive topic of discussion whenever the Indian team management has sat down to finalise the playing XI. It is a position that has consumed the most mind space and yielded the bare minimum returns.Whether it is picking Nitish Kumar Reddy and Shardul Thakur in Tests, or accommodating a spin-bowling all-rounder in Washington Sundar, or more recently Naman Dhir, in white-ball cricket, these resources have invariably been underused.For instance, Dhir was parachuted into the playing XI during West Indies’ ongoing white-ball tour of India. He has earned his stripes as a batter, but both Shubman Gill in ODIs and Shreyas Iyer in T20Is have primarily used him for his off-spinning abilities. While he has looked like a spinner who can effectively chip in to make up for the fifth bowler, the true purpose of his inclusion is yet to be established.In this scenario, Kuldeep Yadav has found himself caught in the crossfire. After the end of the ODI series, Gill was blunt in his admission that the team management was willing to try as many options as possible to find someone who could bat and bowl at No. 8.He categorically mentioned that Anshul Kamboj and Auqib Nabi would remain in the mix because of their batting skills.The fact is that the No. 8 batter has barely managed to make any impact with the ball. And by the time the No. 8 comes out to bat, he has very little room to alter the course of the game.Yet, it appears that the team management is obsessed with the idea that the balance of the XI depends on the player who bats at No. 8.The majority of the matches India have lost during this period have been because of the excessive burden on the batters to put up a score well beyond par in the prevailing conditions. The question that arises here is whether India should consider bringing in a specialist attacking bowler who could restrict the opposition to a lower score, especially on the batting-friendly pitches at home.India’s problems stem from the fact that the team does not have a genuine all-rounder besides the injury-proneHardik Pandya , who can be equally effective with the ball as the third seamer in white-ball cricket and as a batter who can comfortably be sent in to bat in the middle order.Pandya’s back-up project, Reddy, has shown flashes of promise as a lower-order finisher, but his bowling cannot make up for the absence of a third seamer. It is an irony that a position traditionally meant for a specialist bowler is now being decided on the basis of batting skills.India enjoyed a potent pace-bowling attack until the 2023 World Cup, complemented by established spinners. Gill did not fail to mention how much that makes a difference to a line-up. Evidently, India’s white-ball set-up does not have that luxury at the moment.While the next marquee T20 assignment is two years away, the team management does not have much time to find the right combination before next year’s ODI World Cup in Africa.
Article Summary: The No. 8 spot in the batting line-up has been a sensitive topic of discussion. Kuldeep Yadav has found himself caught in the crossfire. India’s problems stem from the fact that the team does not have a genuine all-rounder besides the injury-proneHardik Pandya.

Former India spinner R Ashwin has criticised the team management for dropping Kuldeep Yadav during the ongoing T20I series against the West Indies, questioning the decision to leave out a wrist-spinner who had troubled the visiting batters.Kuldeep featured in the first two matches in Lucknow and Ranchi before being left out of the playing XI for the games in Indore and Hyderabad. He returned figures of 2/33 in the opening T20I but conceded 53 runs in the second match, which India went on to lose.India’s bowling concerns persisted in the fourth T20I in Hyderabad, where the West Indies piled up 247 runs in 20 overs and secured a 24-run victory. Reacting to Kuldeep’s omission, Ashwin said he could not understand why the team management had seemingly lost confidence in the spinner.“It is very surprising because, on a ground where you expect to get some bounce, I know it has not always been a happy hunting ground for spinners, but the West Indies batters are struggling to pick his googly and leg-spin,” Ashwin said on his YouTube channel.He questioned the logic behind excluding Kuldeep against an opposition that had found it difficult to read his variations, adding, “So, if you are leaving Kuldeep out against them, it lacks a bit of common sense.”Ashwin also emphasised the potential impact of Kuldeep’s presence, suggesting that the spinner could have helped restrict the West Indies’ total. “It is very surprising because I think his presence could have made a difference of 15-20 runs,” he said.While Ashwin acknowledged that leaving Kuldeep out in Indore was understandable given the ground’s small dimensions, he rejected the suggestion that the spinner’s performance was responsible for India’s defeat in Ranchi.“I was surprised. Kuldeep was not picked in Indore, and I would still endorse that decision because I can understand that the ground is small,” Ashwin explained.However, he disagreed with attributing the Ranchi defeat to Kuldeep, stating, “But you are almost making an issue out of it by suggesting that India’s loss in Ranchi was because of Kuldeep. That, in itself, is wrong.”Kuldeep had previously impressed during India’s ODI series against the West Indies earlier in the month, claiming seven wickets across three matches to emerge as India’s leading wicket-taker in the series.With the T20I contest level at 2–2, India and the West Indies are set to meet in the fifth and final match in Bengaluru.
Article Summary: Kuldeep was left out of the playing XI for the games in Indore and Hyderabad. He returned figures of 2/33 in the opening T20I but conceded 53 runs in the second match, which India went on to lose. The West Indies piled up 247 runs in 20 overs and secured a 24-run victory.

Article Text:

Out-of-favour India women's cricket team top-order batter Punam Raut on Thursday announced her retirement from all forms of international cricket with immediate effect.The 37-year-old represented India in four Tests, 73 ODIs and 35 T20Is between 2009 and 2021.“After much thought and reflection, I have decided to retire from international cricket in all formats of the game,” Raut said in a post on her Instagram page."Representing India has been the greatest honour of my life. Cricket has been more than just a sport — it has shaped my character, taught me resilience, and given me memories that I will cherish forever. Every time I wore the India jersey, I did so with immense pride and gratitude.“Wearing the India jersey was a dream that became a reality, and I will always be grateful for the trust and support I received.”Raut also thanked the Mumbai Cricket Association for its role in her development as a cricketer.“My sincere thanks to the Mumbai Cricket Association for believing in me during my formative years. The opportunities and guidance I received there laid the foundation of my cricketing journey,” Raut said.She scored 2,299 runs in 73 ODIs, 719 runs in 35 T20Is and 264 runs in four Tests. Her international career included four centuries — three in ODIs and one in a Test against South Africa in 2014 — along with 15 ODI half-centuries and four in T20Is. Her last international appearance was in an ODI against England in June 2021.One of Raut's most memorable performances came during India's run to the 2017 Women's World Cup final. She scored 381 runs in the tournament, including 86 against England in the final at Lord's, which India lost by nine runs.During the same World Cup, Raut scored 109 against Ireland and shared a record 320-run opening partnership with Deepti Sharma.In 2021, Raut was part of India's historic pink-ball Test against Australia. She scored 36 in the first innings and earned praise for walking off after edging a delivery despite being given not out.
Article Summary: Punam Raut has announced her retirement from all forms of international cricket. The 37-year-old represented India in four Tests, 73 ODIs and 35 T20Is between 2009 and 2021. Her international career included four centuries and 15 ODI half- centuries. She scored 381 runs in the 2017 Women's World Cup final.

Article Title: Rohit Sharma's 5th T20I century and two super overs: A look at what happened when India last played in Bengaluru as IND vs WI set for series decider at Chinnaswamy
Article Text:
Rohit Sharma plays a shot during the third T20 cricket match between India and Afghanistan, at M Chinnaswamy Stadium, in Bengaluru. (PTI Photo)

What happened when India last played a T20I in Bengaluru

Shai Hope struck another century as West Indies beat India by 24 runs in the fourth Twenty20 in Hyderabad on Wednesday to level the five-match series at 2-2.Chasing 248, India got off to a quick start, with Sanju Samson reaching his half-century in just 20 balls before Keemo Paul dismissed him for 56.Shreyas Iyer added 16 off 11 balls, while Abhishek Sharma scored 29 before Gudakesh Motie sent the opener back. India mounted another push towards the end through Nitish Kumar Reddy and Tilak Varma, who put together 70 runs off just 32 balls to keep the chase alive.Varma was dismissed for 43, while Paul removed Reddy and took two more wickets in the 19th over, bringing India's chase to a halt. The lower order could not offer much resistance as India were bowled out for 223.Bengaluru will host the series-deciding T20I on Saturday.India last played a T20I in Bengaluru on January 17, 2024, when they faced Afghanistan in the third and final match of the series. India had already secured the series by winning the first two games.But the final match was far from a dead rubber. It produced a series of dramatic moments, including two Super Overs and a controversial episode involving Rohit Sharma.In the first Super Over, Afghanistan's Mohammad Nabi and Rahmanullah Gurbaz ran extra runs after the ball deflected off Nabi's body on the final delivery. The incident left Virat Kohli angry, with the India batter seen clapping in Nabi's face.The drama continued moments later. With two runs needed off the final ball of first super over, Rohit, who was at the non-striker's end, walked off to allow Rinku Singh to take over the running. However, Yashasvi Jaiswal's bottom edge went straight to the wicketkeeper, and India could manage only a single, leaving the first Super Over tied.Rohit was ready to bat again in the second Super Over. Under point 22 of Appendix F of the playing conditions, a batter who had retired could return only if the retirement had been due to injury, illness or "any other unavoidable cause".Earlier in the match, Rohit had won the toss and elected to bat. India suffered a disastrous start, losing four wickets inside the powerplay. Jaiswal fell at 18 in the third over, Kohli was dismissed at the same score in the fourth, Shivam Dube departed at 21, and India lost their fourth wicket at 22.Rohit kept the innings together and combined with Rinku for a 190-run partnership for the fifth wicket. India recovered from 22/4 to finish at 212/4, with Rohit scoring 121 off 69 balls and Rinku making 69 off 38 deliveries.Rohit became the first batter to score five centuries in T20 internationals, rescuing India from a position where they had lost four wickets for just 22 runs.Afghanistan matched India's total, forcing the match into a Super Over. Gulbadin Naib led their fightback with 55 off 23 balls.Naib and Gurbaz came out to bat in the first Super Over, which was bowled by Mukesh Kumar. A mix-up between the batters resulted in Naib being run out. Gurbaz and Nabi then scored runs before the controversial final delivery.The batters ran a bye, but the throw from wicketkeeper Sanju Samson deflected off Nabi's leg towards long-on. The pair ran two more runs. Rohit and his teammates were unhappy with the outcome, though the running was within the rules.India needed 17 runs to win the first Super Over. Rohit hit Azmatullah Omarzai for two successive sixes to leave India needing three runs off the final two balls. With two runs required from the last delivery, Rohit retired hurt to allow Rinku, the quicker runner, to take over. But Jaiswal could only edge the ball towards the wicketkeeper, and India managed just one run, leaving the Super Over tied.By the time the second Super Over began, Rohit had already spent a long time at the crease. He nevertheless hit Fareed Ahmad for a six and a four to give India a strong start. Rinku was dismissed off the first ball, however, and Samson then ran Rohit out, leaving Afghanistan with a target of 12.India handed the ball to leg-spinner Ravi Bishnoi, and he delivered under pressure. Nabi flat-batted a short delivery straight to the fielder at long-off on the first ball, while Gurbaz fell on the third delivery after attempting a similar shot.India won the second Super Over to seal the match after one of the most eventful finishes in T20I cricket.
Article Summary: West Indies beat India by 24 runs to level five-match series at 2-2. India had already secured the series by winning the first two games. Match produced a series of dramatic moments, including two Super Overs. Rohit Sharma became the first batter to score five centuries in T20 internationals.

Zimbabwe's ODI and T20I captain Sikandar Raza has made it clear that his country's possible entry into the World Test Championship (WTC) for the 2027-30 cycle will not change his plan to retire after next year's 50-over World Cup in Africa.Zimbabwe will co-host the 2027 ODI World Cup with South Africa and Namibia. For the 40-year-old all-rounder, the tournament will offer an opportunity to play a World Cup on home soil towards the end of his career.“The fact that I am coming to the end of my career as well, and to have an opportunity to play a home World Cup is certainly a blessing for me from a personal point of view,” Raza said, as quoted by news agency PTI.“Every cricketer dreams of having retired or to retire after playing a cricketing World Cup,” he added.When asked whether Zimbabwe's potential entry into the WTC during the 2027-30 cycle could make him reconsider his retirement, Raza ruled out the possibility.“Would I be tempted? No, I will not be tempted. I have come to peace with the decisions that I am making in life.“I'll not be a guy who will, when the time comes, call it off and then say, 'I'm taking my retirement back.' It will not happen. That's not me,” he said.While Raza does not intend to extend his career, he believes playing in the WTC would help Zimbabwe improve as a cricketing nation.He said the team might take time to perform well in the competition initially, but the experience would help improve its results across formats.“If that happens, I will be the first guy who will be in support of that. If Zimbabwe is part of WTC, we might not be able to do well at the start, but one thing I do know…our cricketing growth eventually — not eventually, quickly — will go up. Our performances will get better, and not just in Test cricket,” he said.Raza acknowledged that Zimbabwe, South Africa and Namibia could find it difficult to gain a home advantage at the 2027 World Cup, as the International Cricket Council (ICC) oversees the tournament's arrangements.“We'll try our best to gain some home advantage, but for ICC events, it's very difficult because the ICC is in control of everything.“But yeah, we will try and take some advantage where we can. Fair advantage, that is,” he said.Zimbabwe's match against India on October 24, 2027, will also be the first World Cup fixture at the newly built Mosi-oa-Tunya International Cricket Stadium in Victoria Falls.
Article Summary: Zimbabwe will co-host the 2027 ODI World Cup with South Africa and Namibia. Sikandar Raza will retire after next year's 50-over World Cup in Africa. The 40-year-old all-rounder believes playing in the WTC would help Zimbabwe improve as a cricketing nation.

Article Title: 'Why attack the batter?': Sunil Gavaskar fumes as Shamar Joseph hits Arshdeep Singh
Article Text:
Sunil Gavaskar and Arshdeep Singh (Image credit: X)

Former India captain Sunil Gavaskar criticised West Indies fast bowler Shamar Joseph after a delivery struck Arshdeep Singh on the shoulder during the fourth T20I in Hyderabad on Wednesday. Gavaskar also called on India's batters to take greater responsibility after the hosts lost the match by 24 runs. The defeat levelled the five-match series and set up a decider in Bengaluru on Saturday.West Indies scored 247 for three before bowling India out for 223. Keemo Paul took five wickets, while captain Shai Hope led the visitors with an unbeaten 102 off 50 balls.The incident took place towards the end of India's chase. A bouncer from Joseph hit Arshdeep on the shoulder, leaving the Indian pacer in pain.Despite the discomfort, Arshdeep continued batting with India needing 30 runs off the final ball. Captain Shreyas Iyer also urged him to retire hurt and leave the field, but Arshdeep chose to stay.On the next delivery, Arshdeep moved away from his stumps and tried to hit the ball for a boundary. Joseph bowled another short delivery towards his injured shoulder. This time, the ball missed Arshdeep and went away for four byes and a wide.Joseph's approach drew a sharp reaction from Gavaskar in the commentary box. The former India captain questioned why the West Indies pacer was bowling at the batter when his stumps were left unprotected."He is aiming at him," Gavaskar was heard saying on air. "Why attack the batter when the stumps are right there?"“If he is not ok, he should retire. He seems to be in pain. You do not want to aggravate that injury,” said Gavaskar.“Would it not be simpler to just aim at the stumps? He knows that he is moving away to the left. Just aim at the stumps. Don’t aim at him. He is aiming at him,” a furious Gavaskar saidArshdeep could not continue after the incident and was retired hurt on five. His injury could be a concern for India ahead of Saturday's series decider.Gavaskar also expressed concern over India's batting performance during the chase. Despite a quick start from Sanju Samson, the hosts failed to reach the target.The former captain said the batting unit needed to improve its approach when chasing big totals.“The first thing this Indian side needs to improve is how they chase. The batting unit needs to show more responsibility. If the batters don’t take responsibility, this Indian side will not succeed,” Gavaskar told JioStar.He felt India should have shown greater control with the bat, especially in conditions that were expected to help the chasing side.“On a pitch like this, with the dew coming in, you have to show the kind of dominance with the bat that a back-to-back T20 World Cup winning team should, but that was missing completely in this game,” he added.The fourth T20I win levelled the series, leaving both teams with everything to play for in the fifth and final match.The series decider will be played at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium in Bengaluru on Saturday.
Article Summary: Sunil Gavaskar criticises Shamar Joseph for bowling at Arshdeep Singh. India lost fourth T20I by 24 runs to West Indies in Hyderabad. The defeat levelled the series and set up a decider in Bengaluru on Saturday.

NEW DELHI: Para cycling chief coach Aditya Mehta on Wednesday withdrew from the Indian contingent for the Aichi-Nagoya Para Asian Games in protest after eligible cyclists were denied selection. Arshad Shaik is now the lone cyclist to travel to Japan, with only a technician for support.Mehta, who has spent 13 years developing Indian para cycling, said he could not abandon athletes whose “hard-earned opportunities have been taken away”. Mehta will stay back in India while sending Shaik with technician Ramesh Pandi, along with the necessary equipment and technical guidance.“I need to stand by my other athletes, who have worked equally hard but have been denied their opportunity to compete at the Games,” Mehta told TOI, warning that the decision could jeopardise India’s Los Angeles Paralympic qualification prospects.He said India’s Asian rankings — seventh in the men’s category and fourth in the women’s — underline the importance of competing and accumulating points at crucial international events. The actual impact on qualification will depend on the applicable rules and final slot allocation.In a late reprieve, the sports ministry approved two Boccia athletes, Sachin Chamaria and Anjali Devi, for the individual events after initially withholding clearance.Their inclusion takes India’s athlete strength to 168, with 112 men and 56 women competing across 11 disciplines. The overall contingent now stands at 281, including 113 officials.India’s para athletes have also been hit by delayed clearances, triggering a logistical scramble with direct flights to Nagoya no longer available and fares reportedly soaring to five times their usual levels.Athletes now are flying to Tokyo before undertaking a roughly four-hour bus journey to Nagoya, TOIhas learnt. The late bookings leave little time for recovery after the long journey, with some events beginning on Friday.
Article Summary: Para cycling chief coach Aditya Mehta withdraws from the Indian contingent for the Aichi-Nagoya Para Asian Games in protest. Arshad Shaik is now the lone cyclist to travel to Japan, with only a technician for support. Boccia gets last-minute clearance for individual events.

Article Title: Hokato and Soman chase Asian Para Games gold
Article Text:
(From left) Soman Rana with Hokato Hotozhe Sema and coach Rakesh Rawat

KOLKATA: Nagaland’s Hokato Hotozhe Sema heads into the Para Asian Games carrying both confidence and a touch of uncertainty. The world No. 2 shot putter in the F57 category was in good shape before an injury disrupted his preparations.“It was a minor injury near the hip region. I did the required exercises and it’s fine now. I am confident of achieving my personal best,” said the Paris Paralympics bronze medallist.While he may not have had the smoothest build-up to the Games, 2026 has still been a memorable year for Hokato. The 42-year-old became world No. 1 in his category and also set a national record with a massive throw of 15.21m at the Indian Open Para Athletics Championships in Bengaluru.But Hokato knows that if he is to stand atop the podium, he may have to get past a familiar face: Soman Rana.Ranked world No. 3, 43-year-old Soman Rana arrives at the Asian Para Games as the reigning Commonwealth Games champion and a two-time World Championships silver medallist, having finished runner-up in 2024 and 2025.The pair have trained together at the Army Paralympic Node in Pune since 2017 under coach Rakesh Rawat, developing both a strong friendship and a fierce rivalry.“We’re very close friends. We eat together, train together and spend a lot of time together. Our coordination is excellent,” said Soman, who suffered a mine blast injury while serving with the 2/8 Gorkha Rifles along the Line of Control in Jammu & Kashmir on Dec 1, 2006.For Hokato that friendship comes with an added competitive edge. “There is definitely a lot of competitiveness. We train together and help each other improve, but once competition starts, everyone wants to win,” he said.Rawat believes that rivalry has been one of the biggest reasons behind their development on the international stage.“They motivate each other a great deal,” Rawat said. “Training together gives them valuable experience. They are friends and support each other, but once competition begins, friendship takes a back seat and they become rivals. The one who performs best on the day wins.”The coach expects both throwers to be in contention for medals and insists there is little to separate them. “The rivalry between them has helped both improve. They are very closely matched. On the day, it could go either way,” he said.Soman agrees, although his Commonwealth Games gold is likely to provide an added boost. “The gold gave me a lot of confidence. But I’ve been in this sport for many years. My confidence was already there and winning the medal only strengthened it,” he said.While both athletes believe a podium finish is within reach, neither is willing to predict who will come out on top.For Hokato, however, a gold medal would carry special significance. Since winning bronze in Paris, the road has not been easy. His father passed away last Dec, while he has also been overseeing the construction of a house in his village of P. Vihoto in Nagaland and supporting his daughter, who recently began an MBA programme in Pune.On the field, injuries disrupted his season and forced him to miss the World Para Athletics Grand Prix in New Delhi. Yet, despite the setbacks, Hokato has remained focused on recovery and training.“Recovery is crucial. If you don’t recover properly, there’s no point competing. You can travel all that way and still return empty-handed,” he said.Now, he is eager to return to competition and renew his rivalry with Soman on one of para athletics’ biggest stages. For India, it could be an ideal scenario: two close friends pushing each other every day in training before battling for continental glory when it matters most.
Article Summary: Hokato Hotozhe Sema is the world No. 2 shot putter in the F57 category. Soman Rana is the reigning Commonwealth Games champion. The pair have trained together at the Army Paralympic Node in Pune since 2017.

NEW DELHI: India will send 166 athletes across 10 disciplines to the 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan , with the Sports Ministry approving a 275-member contingent for the continental event scheduled from October 18 to 24. Para-athletics accounts for the largest share, with 62 athletes, followed by para-badminton with 28 and para-swimming with 16. Para-shooting has 13 athletes, while para-archery and para-table tennis have 11 and 10, respectively.The remaining disciplines are blind football (10), para-powerlifting (eight), para-judo (seven), and para-cycling (one).Sheetal Devi, a double gold medallist at the previous Asian Para Games, will headline India's archery contingent alongside 18-year-old Payal Nag.
